basis: Past, present, and future held in the mind
note: The commentary argues that lived time consists of joined pieces rather than a single flat flow; Augustine describes a present of remembered past, attended present, and expected future, offering a later Christian account of how those parts are connected.

basis: lamps burning; be ready because the hour is unknown
note: The commentary joins night/day divisions to patience and waiting; the Didache tells its readers to watch their lives, keep lamps lit, and be ready because the Lord's hour is unknown, giving the temporal image an early Christian practice of vigilance.

basis: Keep watch because the hour is unknown
note: The commentary stretches patience through uncertain time before the final contraction; the Didache tells believers to watch their lives and keep lamps ready since they do not know the Lord's hour.

basis: Meet often; faith must endure to the end
note: The commentary connects repeated meetings among people with the need to remain through time; the Didache urges frequent gathering for the soul and says a lifetime of faith is of no benefit unless completed at the end.

basis: reprove one another in peace
note: The commentary's reciprocal counsel is tied to haqq; the Didache directs members to reprove each other without anger and in peace, specifying both correction and its manner.

basis: pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day
note: The commentary sets dawn/evening and night/day as named units; the Didache schedules a repeated Christian prayer three times through the day, giving temporal divisions a liturgical practice.

basis: seek the Living One while alive
note: The commentary emphasizes the shortness of life and its closing encounter; this saying urges seeking the Living One before death, turning limited lifetime into an immediate obligation. English wording varies by translation.

basis: love rejoices with truth
note: The commentary couples mutual counsel with haqq; Paul makes truth the object of love's rejoicing, locating truth inside a durable ethical relation.

basis: love endures all things
note: The commentary couples haqq with sabr; Paul describes love as enduring all things, placing endurance inside the same ethical frame as truth in the preceding verse.

basis: If the dead do not rise, eat and drink
note: The commentary reports deniers who treat mortal time as final; Paul voices the practical conclusion of denying resurrection, eating and drinking because tomorrow brings death, then challenges that premise in his resurrection argument.

basis: steadfast work is not in vain
note: The commentary says human beings lose time except through faith and good deeds; in a chapter about resurrection, Paul urges steadfast work because labor in the Lord is not in vain, answering the fear that time erases action.

basis: Steadfastness joined to enduring work
note: The commentary's remaining group combines persistence with righteous deeds; Paul concludes his resurrection argument by telling believers to be steadfast and always active in the Lord's work because that labor is not futile.

basis: The remaining time is shortened
note: The commentary says a long life is seen as compressed when its end approaches; Paul tells believers the appointed time has grown short and therefore their ordinary life relations must be held lightly.

basis: The present form of the world is passing
note: The commentary says a seemingly stable span is already vanishing; Paul tells those engaged with the world not to live as though its present form were lasting.

basis: Fathers and young people addressed separately
note: The commentary names distinct stages of a life; the letter addresses fathers and young people with different spiritual descriptions, an analogy through communal age categories rather than a literal lifespan sequence.

basis: Human flesh as grass
note: The commentary reduces a human lifetime to a passing interval; Peter applies Isaiah's fading-grass image to all flesh, making mortal brevity part of his appeal to a community born through the gospel.

basis: Enduring word against passing life
note: The commentary joins short human life to truth that can hold people together; Peter completes the Isaiah citation by contrasting fading humanity with the Lord's enduring word and identifies that word with what was proclaimed to his hearers.

basis: work of faith; labor of love; endurance of hope
note: The commentary names faith, good works, and patience as the actions of those who escape loss; Paul recalls this community's work, labor, and endurance in faith, love, and hope, preserving the same linked ethical pattern.

basis: Night-and-day prayer seeks to strengthen others
note: The commentary makes mutual support stretch through both parts of the day; Paul describes earnest night-and-day prayer to see his hearers again and supply what their faith lacks.

basis: Times and seasons introduce the final Day
note: The commentary moves from named periods to a sudden terminal hour; Paul explicitly invokes times and seasons before describing the Lord's Day as unexpectedly arriving in the following verse.

basis: Encourage and build one another
note: The commentary's repeated reciprocal counsel makes a durable community; Paul explicitly tells believers to encourage one another and build one another up.

basis: admonish, encourage, support; be patient with all
note: The commentary distinguishes counsel in truth from counsel in patience; Paul assigns different kinds of mutual care and closes with patience toward all, a close ethical configuration of the paired exhortations.

basis: Admonish, help, and be patient with all
note: The commentary couples mutual counsel with patience; this instruction names admonishing the idle, helping the weak, and being patient with everyone as communal practices.

basis: Day of the Lord arrives during night
note: The commentary juxtaposes the day-night pair with the sudden end of a seeming long stay; Paul says the Lord's day comes like a thief in the night, challenging complacency about the remaining time.

basis: Believers belong to day, not night
note: The commentary makes remaining people a distinct group amid the alternation of night and day; Paul calls believers children of light and day, assigning the temporal images an ethical identity.

basis: Wakefulness instead of sleep
note: The commentary develops short sleep and patient alertness across time; Paul tells the community not to sleep as others do but to keep awake and sober in view of the approaching day.

basis: Rich are to become rich in good works
note: The commentary contrasts accumulating possessions with righteous action that endures; Paul instructs the rich to be rich in good works and generous to others.

basis: Store a foundation for the future life
note: The commentary's accumulation motif ends at the grave unless joined to right deeds; Paul pictures generosity as storing a firm foundation for the future so that people may grasp true life.

basis: Outer decline, daily inner renewal
note: The commentary tracks bodily life through aging while patience persists across days; Paul says the outer person wastes away but the inner person is renewed day by day.

basis: Now is the accepted time and day of rescue
note: The commentary's finite interval calls for righteous response before the end; Paul applies a promise about the favorable time and salvation day to his hearers' present now.

basis: Divine patience counted as salvation
note: The commentary joins the waiting interval to the chance to remain among the saved; Peter explicitly asks readers to regard the Lord's patience as salvation, supplying the purpose of the delay.

basis: one day like a thousand years; a thousand years like one day
note: The commentary says the entire lifespan becomes an evening or a day-hour; Peter cites the Lord's different scale of time, explicitly comparing a day with a millennium.

basis: One day and a thousand years
note: The commentary contrasts long duration with its apparent contraction; this verse reversibly compares one day and a thousand years before the Lord, relativizing ordinary measures of waiting.

basis: Delayed promise and divine patience
note: The commentary connects patience to the true promise through a shrinking lifetime; this verse says the promised coming is not slow as some reckon but delayed in divine patience to allow repentance.

basis: Night-and-day labor spares the community
note: The commentary connects righteous work across the daily cycle with people sustaining one another; Paul says his group worked night and day so they would burden none of the believers.

basis: Exhort at every season with patience
note: The commentary's counsel and patience fill successive times; the charge to proclaim the word in season and out of season includes correction and exhortation with complete patience and teaching.

basis: Companionship sought before winter
note: The commentary links winter's coming with people maintaining one another through time; Paul urges his addressee to come before winter, making the seasonal deadline matter for their meeting.

basis: Appointed periods for human peoples
note: The commentary divides time into assigned intervals while people remain joined; Paul says God made every nation from one and determined their appointed times and dwelling boundaries.

basis: Three years of night-and-day admonition
note: The commentary ties mutual counsel to morning/evening and a lasting interval; Paul recalls three years in which he warned each person night and day with tears.

basis: teach and admonish one another
note: The commentary's tawasaw makes counsel reciprocal; Paul describes a community teaching and admonishing one another through wisdom and song, a communal practice parallel to that reciprocal relation.

basis: Teach and admonish one another
note: The commentary defines the surviving group through mutual counsel; Colossians asks believers to let Christ's word dwell among them as they teach and admonish one another wisely.

basis: Speaking truth together builds maturity
note: The commentary makes counsel in truth a way people are joined; speaking truth in love is the means by which members grow toward their common head, Christ.

basis: The body joined by every working part
note: The commentary says the people who remain are added to one another; the body is joined and held together as each part works, building itself up in love.

basis: speak truth to neighbor; members of one another
note: The commentary pairs mutual counsel with haqq; Paul commands truthful speech to a neighbor because the speakers are members of one another, making truth-telling the practice that sustains their shared body.

basis: Speak truth as members of one another
note: The commentary brings truth and people being joined into one image; Ephesians gives membership in one body as the reason for each person to speak truth to a neighbor.

basis: make the most of the time
note: The commentary says number-chasing consumes time unnoticed and that good action matters within a short life; Paul tells readers to make the most of the time because the days are evil, turning the finite span into an ethical opportunity.

basis: Use the time because days are evil
note: The commentary makes limited time the setting for righteous action; Ephesians asks its hearers to make the most of the time because the days are evil.

basis: Present opportunity used for good to all
note: The commentary says righteous deeds and mutual support occupy limited time; Paul says that while opportunity remains believers should do good to everyone, especially fellow believers.

basis: doing good; harvest at the proper time; do not give up
note: The commentary joins righteous deeds to mutual exhortation and patience; Paul says not to tire of doing good because harvest comes at the proper time if one does not give up, joining all three actions in one claim.

basis: Good action sustained until its season
note: The commentary joins righteous deeds and patience across time; Paul says not to grow weary in doing good because a harvest will come at its proper time if people do not give up.

basis: consider one another; provoke love and good works
note: The commentary says people join through reciprocal exhortation and righteous action; Hebrews makes the relation active by telling readers to consider one another and stir up love and good works.

basis: Stir one another to good works
note: The commentary makes shared righteous action part of how people remain connected; Hebrews asks believers to consider one another so as to provoke love and good deeds.

basis: encourage one another as the Day approaches
note: The commentary joins human exhortation to long time and the final gathering; Hebrews commands mutual encouragement as the Day draws near, making the approaching end a reason to remain connected.

basis: Gather and encourage as the Day approaches
note: The commentary connects communal exhortation to passing time; Hebrews opposes abandoning assembly and urges increasingly mutual encouragement as the approaching Day is seen.

basis: endurance after doing God's will; receive the promise
note: The commentary couples patience with right action; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will in order to receive what was promised, making persistence the bridge between action and outcome.

basis: Endurance receives the promised thing
note: The commentary joins patience to the true promise; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will so that hearers may receive what was promised.

basis: present pain; later fruit of righteousness
note: The commentary links sabr with cold and waiting and gives righteous action as the survivor's practice; Hebrews says discipline later yields peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it, explicitly making endurance fruitful over time.

basis: daily exhortation of one another
note: The commentary's tawasaw is reciprocal counsel within a chain; Hebrews says to exhort one another every day so none is hardened, adding a daily rhythm and a reason for the practice.

basis: Exhort one another every day
note: The commentary's people remain joined through reciprocal counsel across linked days; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation while it is called Today, to prevent hardening through sin.

basis: A new Today after a long time
note: The commentary describes time as linked parts in which an appeal remains open; Hebrews says God appoints another day called Today after a long time, using David's warning to demand a present response.

basis: inherit promises through faith and patience
note: The commentary's exception to loss joins faith, righteous action, and sabr; Hebrews urges imitation of those who inherit the promises through faith and patience, aligning endurance with promised outcome.

basis: Abraham waited patiently and received the promise
note: The commentary ties sabr to waiting for an outcome; Hebrews says Abraham patiently endured and obtained the promise, giving a narrative example of long waiting rewarded.

basis: The rich fade in the midst of pursuits
note: The commentary says acquisitive effort can consume the person's unnoticed time; James likens a rich person's fading during pursuits to a flower withered by the rising sun.

basis: faith tested produces endurance
note: The commentary names faith and sabr together; James says the testing of faith produces endurance, giving patience a process rather than treating it as a static trait.

basis: endurance brought to completion
note: The commentary says patient persistence carries people through time; James tells endurance to complete its work so that the person may be mature and whole, linking duration to ethical formation.

basis: Merchants plan a profitable year
note: The commentary recalls competitive accumulation that hides life's shortness; James addresses people planning a year of travel and trade for gain, the precise plan exposed as uncertain in the next verse.

basis: Life appears briefly and vanishes
note: The commentary reduces a seeming long residence to a small interval; James calls human life a vapor that appears a little while and disappears, addressing people who plan future years.

basis: Prophets as examples of patient speech
note: The commentary couples truth-telling with endurance; James names prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience.

basis: farmer waits patiently for the earth's crop
note: The commentary explains sabr as waiting and names winter/seasonal time; James tells readers to be patient like a farmer waiting for the earth's precious crop and its early and late rains.

basis: Farmer waits through seasonal rains
note: The commentary names winter's severity and the waiting that spans seasons; James asks believers to be patient like a farmer waiting for precious fruit through early and late rain until the Lord's coming.

basis: establish hearts; the Lord's coming is near
note: The commentary stretches patience across the day and compresses life at its end; James commands steadfast hearts because the Lord's coming is near, joining endurance to an approaching end.

basis: Twelve hours mark the usable day
note: The commentary treats the day as a bounded segment in which one's way matters; Jesus asks whether the day has twelve hours and connects walking without stumbling to its light.

basis: The dead rise according to deeds
note: The commentary's final compressed stay ends in loss for deniers and survival through right action; Jesus says those in the tombs come out to resurrection of life or judgment according to what they have done.

basis: work while it is day; night comes
note: The commentary pairs day and night and treats human action as a response to finite time; Jesus says the sender's work must be done while it is day because night is coming, giving the daily boundary an explicit urgency for action.

basis: Work during the remaining day
note: The commentary links right deeds to the short allotted interval; Jesus says the works of the sender must be done while it is day, since night comes when no one can work.

basis: Enlarged barns for accumulated goods
note: The commentary recalls multiplying wealth until the grave; the rich man decides to build larger barns to store all his grain and goods before his mortality is exposed in the story.

basis: Possessions imagined to guarantee many years
note: The commentary links the competition to increase possessions with failure to notice time passing; the rich man addresses his soul as though stored goods secured many years of rest.

basis: Stored years collapse into one night
note: The commentary contrasts a lifetime of numerical accumulation with its abrupt end; the rich man's planned many years are cut short that very night, and he is asked who will have his stored goods.

basis: Self-stored goods versus wealth toward God
note: The commentary opposes multiplication of possessions to deeds that endure; Jesus closes the rich fool's story by contrasting storing up for oneself with being rich toward God.

basis: Servants wait to admit the returning master
note: The commentary links people through patient readiness during uncertain time; Jesus compares disciples to servants waiting for their master so they can open immediately when he arrives.

basis: second or third watch; servants found awake
note: The commentary glosses sabr as waiting across time; Jesus blesses servants whom the returning master finds awake in the second or third watch, giving waiting a specific night-time interval.

basis: Faithful waiting through night watches
note: The commentary puts patience across segmented night; Jesus calls servants blessed if found alert when their master comes in the second or third watch.

basis: Elect cry day and night for justice
note: The commentary places truth and patient appeal across daily cycles; Jesus describes God's chosen crying to him day and night for justice in a parable about persistent prayer.

basis: An aged witness awaits a promise before death
note: The commentary sets divine promise within the finite span of a life; Simeon has been told he will not see death before seeing the Messiah, making his later waiting answer a personal life limit.

basis: Prayer and fasting night and day
note: The commentary places steadfast worship across the paired periods; the aged Anna serves in the temple with fasting and prayer night and day, joining old age with continuous devotion.

basis: endurance gains life
note: The commentary says those joined by patience remain standing through time; Jesus says life is gained through endurance, making perseverance the means of survival.

basis: Pray flight will not be in winter
note: The commentary treats winter's cold as a concrete trial inside the calendar; Jesus tells hearers to pray that the expected flight not happen in winter, making season alter the hardship of endurance.

basis: evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning watches
note: The commentary names night/day and dawn/evening pairs and links sabr to waiting; Jesus lists four night watches and tells servants to stay awake for the master's return, making the divided night a scene of patient readiness.

basis: sleeping and rising; growth night and day
note: The commentary's asr discussion includes night/day and sleep in portions, while sabr is waiting; the seed in Jesus' parable sprouts as the farmer sleeps and rises, night and day, joining bodily rest to unobserved duration.

basis: first blade, then ear, then full grain
note: The commentary names stages of a human lifespan and appointed seasons; the parable makes growth a sequence of stages before harvest, a specific image of time unfolding toward ripeness.

basis: harvest when the grain is ripe
note: The commentary connects sabr with waiting; the farmer sends the sickle when the crop is ready, making patient waiting end at its appointed season.

basis: One hour compared with the whole day's labor
note: The commentary compresses a long stay to an hour and asks what deeds count at its end; the first workers complain that those hired last worked only one hour yet received an equal wage, a parabolic comparison rather than a statement that all lives are equally long.

basis: endure to the end and be saved
note: The commentary says those who attach to one another through patience remain standing; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved, giving patience a clear terminal horizon.

basis: Endurance until the end
note: The commentary says those who endure remain through the chain of time; Jesus says the one who endures to the end will be saved, making persistence across the whole interval decisive.

basis: Winter intensifies the coming ordeal
note: The commentary names winter's hard cold as one temporal condition for patience; Jesus tells hearers to pray that their flight does not occur in winter, when that season will worsen their urgent journey.

basis: Prepared attendants enter before the door closes
note: The commentary asks who remains when an apparently long wait abruptly ends; in the bridegroom story those prepared enter the feast on his arrival and the door is shut.

basis: Unknown day and hour demand watchfulness
note: The commentary compresses the end of a long interval into an unexpected moment; the bridegroom parable concludes with an instruction to stay awake because the day and hour are unknown.

basis: Delay produces sleep in a waiting group
note: The commentary gives broken sleep a place between periods of waiting; in Jesus' bridegroom story the delay makes all the attendants drowsy and asleep before the decisive arrival.

basis: endurance, God's commands, and faith
note: The commentary pairs faith and righteous acts with sabr; Revelation defines the endurance of the saints through keeping God's commands and faith, making patience a lived obedience.

basis: Endurance, divine commands, and faith
note: The commentary's surviving group combines belief, deeds, and patience; Revelation characterizes the saints' endurance by keeping God's commandments and faith in Jesus.

basis: deeds follow the dead
note: The commentary reduces a lifetime to the gathering day and asks what survives it; Revelation says the dead rest from their labors and their deeds follow them, giving action an after-death persistence.

basis: faithful to death; crown of life
note: The commentary traces a human span to its end and says the faithful endure; Revelation calls the community to faithfulness even to death and promises the crown of life, linking lifetime's limit to reward.

basis: works, love, faith, service, and endurance
note: The commentary's exception to loss joins faith, good works, and patience; the risen Christ names a church's works, love, faith, service, and endurance together, adding a concrete communal evaluation.

basis: The dead judged from records of deeds
note: The commentary reports that time itself is said to destroy and recalls an accounting after a brief-seeming stay; Revelation has the dead stand before the throne as books are opened and each is judged by deeds.

basis: patient endurance; an approaching hour of testing
note: The commentary stretches patience across time and reduces the final span to an hour; Revelation connects keeping the word of endurance with preservation from an hour of testing that is coming on the world.

basis: The slain ask how long until judgment
note: The commentary connects waiting with a true final reckoning; the slain ask the sovereign Lord how long before he judges and vindicates their blood.

basis: Rest a little longer until number complete
note: The commentary gives patient waiting a finite interval and links the fates of people; the martyrs are told to rest a little longer until their fellow servants are complete.

basis: Communal service day and night
note: The commentary makes daily alternation part of continuing allegiance; the rescued multitude stands before God's throne and serves him day and night, extending joined devotion beyond mortal time.

basis: patient in affliction; constant in prayer
note: The commentary stretches patience across daily prayer times and ties sabr to waiting; Paul joins patience in affliction to constancy in prayer, giving that waiting a devotional form.

basis: Patient affliction with persistent prayer
note: The commentary stretches patience between repeated times of worship; Paul joins patience in tribulation to constancy in prayer as the group's practice.

basis: Night is advanced, day draws near
note: The commentary makes night-to-day transition a call to moral action; Paul says the passing night and approaching day demand casting off dark works and taking up the armor of light.

basis: goodness, knowledge, and ability to admonish one another
note: The commentary joins good action to reciprocal counsel; Paul says the community is filled with goodness and knowledge and able to admonish one another, specifying the qualities that make mutual advice possible.

basis: wait patiently for what is not seen
note: The commentary describes sabr as waiting and directs it toward survival; Paul says hope for what is not seen requires waiting with patience, adding the unseen promise as the object of endurance.

basis: Hope for unseen end requires patience
note: The commentary asks people to wait through an interval for a promised resolution; Paul says those hoping for what they do not yet see wait for it with endurance.

basis: Righteous souls ask how long they must wait
note: The commentary links patient waiting to the final reckoning; the souls of the righteous ask from their chambers when the reward will arrive, making the interval after death itself a question. Numbering of 4 Ezra varies by edition.

basis: Waiting ends when the number is complete
note: The commentary says people remain linked through a long interval before its end; the angel's reply makes the completion of the number of the righteous the limit of their wait. Numbering of 4 Ezra varies by edition.

basis: Evening before morning in prayer order
note: The commentary puts night and day into a deliberate sequence; the discussion explains beginning the daily Shema with evening by appealing to creation's evening followed by morning, turning Genesis' order into a repeated act.

basis: If not now, when; if only for self, what am I
note: The commentary binds short time to the need for others; Hillel's paired questions reject delay and self-enclosure in the same ethical saying.

basis: Fixed instruction must become deeds
note: The commentary couples counsel in truth with righteous works; Shammai says to make Torah study regular, speak little, and do much, specifying how words and acts should be ordered across ordinary time.

basis: Acquire a friend and a teacher
note: The commentary makes people remain linked by guidance; Avot directs a person to make a teacher and acquire a friend, turning endurance into a sustained interpersonal practice.

basis: Continue the work though it cannot be finished
note: The commentary's patient group persists across a life too short to encompass everything; Avot says one need not finish the work but is not free to abandon it.

basis: Do not defer study until free time
note: The commentary says time is spent in successive limited pieces; Avot warns that a hoped-for leisure interval may never come, making present instruction urgent.

basis: Prepare in this life's antechamber
note: The commentary treats mortal time as a bounded span before the final meeting; Avot likens this world to an antechamber where one prepares before entering the coming world's hall.

basis: One hour of repentance and good deeds
note: The commentary says long earthly time contracts to an hour and makes righteous action decisive; Avot values one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world while separately valuing an hour of the coming world's peace.

basis: Named ages of a human life
note: The commentary explicitly parses youth, maturity, and decline as time's pieces; Avot gives a sequence of ages with different pursuits and capacities, including forty for understanding and seventy for old age. Section numbering varies by edition.

basis: evening and morning Shema
note: The commentary names night/day and dawn/evening as paired time units; this Mishnah defines when the evening and morning recitations of Shema begin and end, showing those same boundaries structuring Jewish daily liturgy.

basis: Nighttime recitation has a bounded interval
note: The commentary makes night a distinct period filled with a sustained religious act; the Mishnah asks when the evening Shema is read and sets competing limits within the night's watches.

basis: Morning recitation begins with visible dawn
note: The commentary joins morning to the night before it as a new part of disciplined time; the Mishnah asks when morning Shema begins and uses the ability to distinguish colors to mark the transition.

basis: morning prayer, afternoon prayer, evening prayer
note: The commentary names dawn and evening as paired times; this Mishnah assigns prayer to morning, afternoon, and evening limits, showing daily divisions shaping Jewish worship.

basis: acquire a friend; appoint a teacher; judge favorably
note: The commentary says people are linked by reciprocal counsel; Avot turns that into practices of friendship, learning, and favorable judgment, giving the social chain an ethical form.

basis: the day is short; work is abundant
note: The commentary says the human span contracts to an hour while good action remains its answer; Avot explicitly pairs a short day with abundant work and a pressing master, making ethical urgency the point of the time limit.

basis: work cannot be finished, but one must not desist
note: The commentary links sabr with waiting and persistence across time; Avot says one need not complete the work but is not free to desist, distinguishing perseverance from control over the whole lifespan.

basis: one hour of repentance and good deeds
note: The commentary contrasts long life with a compressed hour and names righteous deeds as a way through loss; Avot says one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the world to come, giving that hour explicit moral weight.

basis: acts whose fruits are enjoyed now and whose principal remains for the world to come
note: The commentary names righteous deeds as the answer to loss and describes people helping one another; the Talmud lists concrete acts such as honoring parents, kindness, hospitality, and peacemaking whose reward extends beyond this life.

basis: Repent one day before death
note: The commentary says a long life can shrink suddenly to its last fraction; the rabbinic explanation of repentance one day before death is to repent each day because no one knows which day will be last.

basis: few years compared with eternity
note: The commentary reduces the whole lifespan to an evening or day-hour; Sirach compares a few years to a drop of water and a grain of sand beside eternity, making the disparity explicit.

basis: Few years beside eternal days
note: The commentary says lengthy human residence looks like only a small daytime fraction; Sirach likens human years against eternity to a drop of sea water or a grain of sand.

basis: human lifespan capped at a hundred years
note: The commentary follows age stages and says a lifetime shrinks to a short interval; Sirach measures human days at most a hundred years, adding a wisdom-text reckoning of the finite span.

basis: Even a century is a small life span
note: The commentary counts human ages and then reduces a whole life to a brief interval; Sirach calls a hundred years a large number of human days before measuring them against eternity.

basis: Gathered festivals rejected without justice
note: The commentary says a community persists through righteous conduct, truth, and patience; Amos has God reject its festivals and solemn assemblies, complicating the assumption that recurring gatherings alone preserve a people.

basis: Justice must flow continually
note: The commentary joins truthful counsel to the group's endurance; after rejecting festivals Amos calls for justice to roll like water and righteousness like an enduring stream, identifying the needed practice beyond assembly.

basis: blessing for waiting through a counted span
note: The commentary says sabr is waiting and the life span contracts to a short interval; Daniel blesses the one who waits and reaches the end of a specified number of days.

basis: Blessed one who waits through counted days
note: The commentary makes endurance stretch over a measured interval; Daniel blesses the person who waits to the specified day count, joining a finite duration to perseverance.

basis: rest, then stand at the end of days
note: The commentary joins death, the gathering day, and the fate of those who endure; Daniel is told to go his way, rest, and rise to his allotted place at the end of days, adding a personal resurrection promise.

basis: sleepers awake; everlasting life or disgrace
note: The commentary compresses human time toward the gathering day and speaks of loss; Daniel describes those sleeping in the dust awakening to divergent everlasting outcomes, adding an explicit resurrection horizon.

basis: The long dead awaken for judgment
note: The commentary's brief-seeming stay ends at a gathering where deniers lose; Daniel says many who sleep in the dust awaken, some to everlasting life and some to shame, supplying a direct alternative to death as time's final word.

basis: wise lead many to righteousness and shine forever
note: The commentary says people attach to one another through exhortation and remain within a chain; Daniel describes the wise who make many righteous shining like stars forever, a transmission of right conduct with enduring outcome.

basis: Three daily prayers despite hostile decree
note: The commentary stretches the act of patience between recurring times of day; Daniel continues praying three times daily even after the written decree against that practice.

basis: commentary root ع ص ر; table's sound correspondence עצר is unverified; festival assembly
note: The commentary labels Arabic العصر for paired periods; Deuteronomy closes six days of unleavened bread with an עֲצֶרֶת, an assembly on the seventh day. The link is a bounded festival time culminating in assembly, while the Hebrew word's assembly sense does not establish cognacy with the Arabic time word.

basis: Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew עצר: seventh-day assembly
note: The table's sound correspondence alone does not establish cognacy; after six days of unleavened bread the seventh is an עצרת, joining a counted sequence to communal gathering as in the commentary's meeting of time and people.

basis: commentary root ح ق ق; table's sound correspondence חקק is unverified; statutes beside righteousness
note: The commentary labels haqq and uses it for right guidance; Deuteronomy places חֻקִּים, prescribed statutes, beside the claim that Israel's instruction is righteous, giving a legal-order use of the table's candidate correspondence without equating prescription with truth.

basis: teach children while sitting, walking, lying down, and rising
note: The commentary joins night/day and develops reciprocal exhortation; Deuteronomy distributes teaching across ordinary daily activities, showing instruction woven through time, though its speaker assigns it parent-to-child rather than mutual counsel.

basis: Teach others at lying down and rising
note: The commentary says people become linked through repeated counsel while time passes; Israel is to teach the words to children while sitting, walking, lying down, and rising.

basis: Sun returns after setting
note: The commentary treats morning and late day as recurring joined pieces; Ecclesiastes has the sun rise, set, and hurry back to the place of its rising.

basis: sow in the morning and keep working at evening
note: The commentary joins morning to evening and speaks of patience while time passes; Qohelet tells the worker to sow in the morning and not hold back at evening, while admitting the outcome is unknown, joining action to uncertain time.

basis: Youth faces later judgment
note: The commentary names youth as one stage and ends with reckoning of a whole life; Ecclesiastes tells the young person to rejoice while young but to know God will bring these acts into judgment.

basis: youth before the evil days

note: The commentary calls winter a particular hard interval and ties waiting to its end; the lover announces that winter and its rain are over, so the harsh season has a bounded duration.

basis: true judgment and compassion toward one another
note: The commentary's final verse has people exhort one another in haqq; Zechariah commands true judgment and compassion each toward a fellow, joining right judgment to reciprocal ethical treatment.

basis: speak truth to one another; judgments in the gates
note: The commentary's tawasaw bil-haqq is mutual counsel in truth; Zechariah explicitly commands people to speak truth to one another and render true, peaceable judgments, adding a public civic setting.

basis: Speak truth to one's neighbor
note: The commentary's mutual counsel is specifically counsel in truth; Zechariah commands each person to speak truth to a neighbor and to render truthful, peace-making judgments.

basis: One group urges another to seek God
note: The commentary's people attach themselves to one another through counsel; the city's inhabitants invite others to go entreat God and add that they themselves will go.

basis: People hold onto another to go together
note: The commentary says people are added to one another through a shared orientation to God; Zechariah imagines people of many languages grasping a Jew's garment and asking to go with him because God is with the group.

basis: Tyre piles silver before its fall
note: The commentary recalls abundance amassed before a terminal reversal; Tyre heaps silver like dust in this verse before its wealth is stripped in the next. Hebrew צבר is the table's sound correspondence to Arabic ṣ-b-r, with no asserted patience cognacy.

basis: short and sorrowful life; no return from Hades
note: The commentary quotes deniers who say time alone destroys them; Wisdom gives the ungodly a speech that life is short and death final, then its larger argument contests their conclusion, adding a Jewish wisdom debate over the denial.

basis: The impious call life short and death final
note: The commentary reports those who think time alone destroys them; Wisdom assigns to its impious speakers the claim that life is short and no remedy follows death, but the book frames their reasoning as unsound.

basis: The impious claim death returns them to nonexistence
note: The commentary recalls the claim that time alone destroys and counters it with final reckoning; Wisdom puts in the impious speakers' mouths the claim that chance brought them into being and afterward they will be as though they had never existed.

basis: life passes like a cloud; name and works forgotten
note: The commentary says time consumes people and their lifespan contracts; the ungodly in Wisdom say their name and works will be forgotten and life passes like a cloud, dramatizing the same fear of erasure.

basis: Life as a passing shadow
note: The commentary says the long stay contracts to an evening or an hour; the impious speakers in Wisdom compare life to a passing shadow, though the book presents their conclusion about death as mistaken.
